source_text: adhuc, inquit, secundum hominem dico: dum essemus paruuli, sub elementis mundi eramus positi ad deseruiendum eis. atquin non est hoc humanitus dictum, non enim exemplum est, sed ueritas. quis enim paruulus — utique sensu, quod sunt nationes — non elementis subiectus est mundi, quae pro deo suspicit? illud autem fuit, quod tum secundum hominem dixit: sed tamen testamentum hominis nemo spernit aut superordinat. exemplo enim humani testamenti permanentis diuinum tuebatur: Abrahae dictae sunt promissiones et semini eius. non dixit \'seminibus*, quasi pluribus, sed \'semini\' tamquam uni, quod est Christus. erubescat spongia Marcionis! nisi quod ex abundanti retracto quae abstulit, cum ualidius sit illum ex his reuinci, quae seruauit. cum autem euenit impleri tempus, misit deus filium suum, utique is, qui etiam ipsorum temporum deus est, quibus saeculum constat, qui signa quoque temporum ordinauit, soles et lunas et sidera et stellas, qui filii denique sui reuelationem in extremitatem temporum et disposuit et praedicauit: in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini, et: in nouissimis diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem, secundum Iohelem. ipsius erat sustinuisse tempus impleri, cuius erat etiam finis temporis sicut initium. ceterum deus ille otiosus nec operationis nec praedicationis ullius atque ita nec temporis alicuius, quid omnino egit, quod efficeret tempus impleri et iam implendum sustineri? si nihil, satis uanum est, ut creatoris tempora sustinuerit seruiens creatori. cui autem rei misit filium suum? ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret - hoc est ut efficeret tortuosa in uiam rectam et aspera in uias leues secundum Esaiam, ut uetera transirent et noua orirentur: lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem — et ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus, utique nationes, quae filii non eramus. et ipse enim erit lux nationum et in nomine eius nationes sperabunt. itaque ut certum esset nos filios dei esse, misit spiritum suum in corda nostra clamantem: abba, pater. in nouissimis enim, inquit, diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem. cuius gratia, nisi cuius et promissio gratiae?
pass_a_gloss: still, he says, I speak according to man: while we were children, we were placed under the elements of the world to serve them. but indeed this is not said in a human way, for it is not an example, but truth. for who, indeed a child - certainly in understanding, because they are nations - is not subject to the elements of the world, which they regard as God? but that was what he said according to man at that time: but nevertheless no one despises or disobeys a human testament. for by the example of a human testament he was defending the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. he did not say 'seeds', as if many, but 'seed', as if one, which is Christ. let Marcion's sponge be ashamed! unless I am retracting from abundance what he took away, since it is more valid to convict him from those things which he preserved. when, however, the time came to be fulfilled, God sent his Son, certainly he who is also the God of those times, by which the age consists, who also arranged the signs of the times, sun and moon and stars, who finally disposed and predicted the revelation of his Son at the end of times: in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and: in the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, according to Joel. it was his to sustain the time to be fulfilled, whose was also the end of time as the beginning. but what did that idle God do, who had no operation or prediction or time, to bring it about that the time was fulfilled and now sustained? if nothing, it is quite vain that he, serving the Creator, sustained the times of the Creator. to what purpose did he send his Son? so that he might redeem those who were under the law - that is, so that he might make the crooked straight and the rough smooth, according to Isaiah, so that the old things might pass away and new things might arise: a new law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem - and so that we might receive the adoption of sons, certainly we nations, who were not sons. and he himself will be the light of the nations and in his name the nations will hope. and so that it might be certain that we are sons of God, he sent his Spirit into our hearts crying: Abba, Father. for in the last days, he says, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. to whose grace, if not to whose promise of grace?

choices.why: to describe a God who does nothing
to indicate the purpose of God's action
to describe the path of those under the law

bible_refs.note: pour out my Spirit on all flesh

pass_b_english: I'm still speaking in human terms, he says: while we were children, we were placed under the elemental powers of the world to serve them. But this isn't merely a human saying; it's not an illustration but the truth. What child — at least in understanding, since the nations are such children — isn't subject to the world's elements, which they worship as gods? That was the point I made in human terms at the time. Still, no one disregards or tampers with a human will. I used the example of a human will to defend the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed (Genesis 17:7-8). Scripture doesn't say 'seeds,' as if many, but 'seed,' as if one — and that one is Christ. Let Marcion's sponge blush with shame! I'm only piling on from the abundance of what he discarded, since it's even more damning to convict him from the very texts he kept.

When the appointed time arrived, God sent his Son — the very one who is also God of those ages that structure the world, who set the heavenly signs in motion, sun and moon and stars alike, who both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the culmination of the ages: 'In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest' (Isaiah 2:2-3), and 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh,' according to Joel (Joel 2:28). It belonged to him to sustain the era until its fulfillment, since both the end and the beginning of time are his. But what did that idle god do — a god with no action, no prophecy, no time of his own — to bring about the fulfillment and sustain the era now due? If nothing, it's utterly empty that he, serving the Creator, merely propped up the Creator's ages.

Why did he send his Son? To redeem those under the law — that is, to straighten the crooked and smooth the rough, as Isaiah says, so the old order passes and the new arises: a new law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isaiah 2:2-3) — and so we might receive adoption as sons, we nations who were not sons. He himself will be the light of the nations, and in his name the nations will hope. So that we might know for certain we are God's children, he sent his Spirit into our hearts crying, 'Abba, Father.' For 'in the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.' Whose grace is this, if not the one whose promise of grace it is?

review.notes: Pass B fails on scripture citations. The Latin text quotes 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' (in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest), which is a reference to Isaiah 2:2. Pass B cites this as 'Isaiah 2:2-3'. However, the text also quotes 'lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem' (a new law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem), which is also Isaiah 2:3. Pass B cites this second part as 'Isaiah 2:2-3'. While the range is technically correct, the first citation in Pass B for 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' is attributed to 'Isaiah 2:2-3', but the text 'in nouissimis diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem' is correctly identified as Joel. The failure is in the first citation: the Latin 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' is a specific clause. More importantly, Pass B's handling of the Isaiah 2:2-3 citation is redundant and potentially misaligned with the specific clause structure. However, the definitive failure is that Pass B provides 'Isaiah 2:2-3' for 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini', but the Latin text does not provide a citation for that specific clause, and the translator has added a citation that, while accurate to the content, must be checked for precision. Looking closer: 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' is Isaiah 2:2. 'lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem' is Isaiah 2:3. Pass B groups them as 'Isaiah 2:2-3' for the first and 'Isaiah 2:2-3' for the second. This is acceptable. The actual error is in the first citation of Pass B: 'In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest' (Isaiah 2:2-3). The Latin 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' is a single clause. The error is that Pass B includes 'Isaiah 2:2-3' for a single clause that is only verse 2. More critically, Pass B's translation of 'superordinat' as 'tampers with' is a significant departure from the sense of 'superordinat' (to set above/order/appoint) and 'non... superordinat' (no one disregards or [sets aside/overrules]), whereas Pass A correctly uses 'despises or disobeys'. 'Tampers with' implies interference, whereas 'superordinat' in this context refers to the authority/order of a testament. However, the primary reason for failure is the scripture citation for 'in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini' being cited as 'Isaiah 2:2-3' when it is specifically verse 2, and the subsequent citation for the Zion/Jerusalem clause also being 'Isaiah 2:2-3'. While not a 'wrong' verse, the instruction says 'Fail missing, shifted, or false citations'. The citation is not false, but the translation of 'superordinat' as 'tampers with' is a failure of agency/doctrine as it changes the nature of the human testament's authority.
reasons: Pass B translates 'non est... superordinat' as 'no one disregards or tampers with', which misrepresents the Latin 'superordinat' (to place above/order/appoint) in the context of a legal testament; 'tampers with' implies a different type of action than the legal standing of a testament described in the source.
